response.translation: Whoever, then, has been properly educated in the Hippocratic doctrines has learned that, of what is by now customarily named by all physicians the insensible [206] transpiration, by which bodies transpire, one kind is such as vapour, another such as dry air, and another falls out together with perceptible moistures. Something is missing. This, then, is the passage from what Lycus has written toward establishing that one hot thing differs in nothing from another, a passage that does not wait for refutation from outside but overthrows itself. For what in fact does he say? ‘The hot, insofar as it is conceived as hot, has no variation with respect to another hot.’ If, then, the phrase ‘insofar as it is conceived as hot’ signifies nothing in the argument, let it be removed from it entirely. But if it does signify something, it still clearly indicates that in this respect the hot does not differ from the hot, but that in some other respect it does differ.

renderings.english: such as (one kind is such as)

response.translation: For if it differs in no way at all, the ‘insofar as’ is added superfluously; but if it differs in some other respect, while in this respect it does not differ, then let the differences be conceived in that respect [207] in which it differs. Since if one were to consider each thing only in the respect in which it is spoken of, you will abolish the differences of all things. The animal, insofar as it is conceived as animal, differs in nothing from another animal. The plant, insofar as it is conceived as plant, differs in nothing from another plant. The tree, insofar as it is conceived as tree, differs in nothing from another tree. Are there then no differences of animal: the winged and the footed and the swimming, and the aquatic and the land-dwelling and the aerial, or the mortal and the immortal, or the rational and the irrational, or the tame and the wild, or the cowardly and the brave, or each of the others that we know? For why speak at length? So too among plants one is a tree, another a shrub, another a thorn, another a herb, another brushwood; or, although all of them, in the respect in which they are conceived as animals, have no difference, would one not nonetheless truly call all these which he has mentioned, and not a few others besides these, differences of animal? And so too in the case of plants.

For a plant does not differ from a plant by one of them being rational [208] and the other irrational, nor by the winged or the footed, nor by any of the other differences mentioned. Just as neither does an animal differ from an animal by one being a shrub, another a thorn, another a tree, another a herb, another brushwood, another a cedar; rather, such a division belongs within the genus of plants. But Lycus himself also writes down a great many differences of diseases, although a disease differs in nothing from a disease insofar as it is a disease, just as neither does a symptom from a symptom insofar as it is a symptom; and yet Lycus undertakes to write down the differences of these too, as indeed also those of pleurisy and of each of the other diseases. And yet pleurisy differs in nothing from pleurisy insofar as it is pleurisy; but nonetheless one kind has its pain terminating at the collar-bone, another at the hypochondrium. So too one of the pleurisies goes with the sputum being coloured, while another, opposite to this one, is called by some ‘without sputum’; and there are many other differences, according to which it comes about that the treatment too is varied.

But it is so even if [209] Lycus attempts to teach these differences of the fevers themselves. And yet whether their generation is by an excess of heat or by the biting character of the quality, there will be no difference of fever from fever insofar as it is fever. So uneducated, then, is the argument Lycus propounds that he does not perceive that he is abolishing all the arts. For it is in the knowledge of the differences of each of the things that are that the arts are constituted. And Plato went through this at greatest length in the Philebus as well, right at the beginning of the treatise; and Aristotle and Theophrastus preserved his opinion, as did Chrysippus and Mnesitheus, and there is no one who did not go through the same argument in his writing On Art. The first passage of Plato concerning the constitution of the arts is stated as follows. Socrates: ‘Sound, as it comes through the mouth, is for us one, I suppose, and again unlimited in multitude, both of all and of each.’ Protarchus: ‘What then?’ Socrates:

‘And we are not yet wise by either of these, neither because we know its unlimited nor because we know its one; but that we know how many [210] they are and of what sort, this is what makes each of us lettered.’ Protarchus: ‘Most true.’ Socrates: ‘And indeed what happens to make a man musical, this is the same thing.’ Protarchus: ‘How so?’ Socrates: ‘Sound, I suppose, is one in itself as regards that art too.’ Protarchus: ‘How could it not be?’ Socrates: ‘And let us posit two, low and high, and as a third the equal-toned; or how?’ Protarchus: ‘So.’ Socrates: ‘But you would not yet be wise in music knowing these things alone, while not knowing them you would be, so to speak, worth nothing in these matters.’ Protarchus: ‘Certainly not.’ Socrates:

renderings.english: so to speak (ὥς γε ἔπος εἰπεῖν)

response.translation: ‘But, my friend, when you have grasped the intervals of sound, how many they are in number, as regards highness and lowness, and of what sort, and the boundaries of the intervals, and how many systems have arisen out of these, which our predecessors discerned and handed down to us their followers, to call them harmoniai; and again that in the movements of the body there are other such affections coming to be, which, when measured by numbers, he says one must name rhythms and [211] metres, and at the same time to understand that this is how one must inquire about every one and many. For when you have grasped these very things in this way, then you have become wise; and when, inquiring in this way, you have got hold of any other of the things that are, you have thus become intelligent about it.’ These things from Plato, then, would have sufficed for hearers possessed of intelligence as a demonstration of the constitution of all the arts. For it is not possible to become skilled in an art, not even in regard to a single thing, without knowing their differences; but it is no worse that, just as Plato himself was not content with the summary argument alone but added examples for the sake of clarity, grammar and music, so we too should add one further example, the art of painting, whose underlying matter is colours. For here too one may of course say that colour differs in nothing from colour insofar as it is colour, and on this ground abolish all the differences among them, which indeed Plato himself has pointed out at the beginning of the Philebus.

For when Socrates was dividing the pleasures, his interlocutor would not concede that they all differ from one another [212] insofar as they are pleasures, asserting that they are most alike; but Socrates meets him with this argument: ‘For indeed colour, my good sir, will in this very respect differ in nothing from colour, by the whole of it being colour; yet we all recognise that black, besides being different from white, is in fact also most opposite to it. And so too figure with figure: in genus it is all one and the same; but of its parts, some are most opposite to one another, while others, I suppose, in fact have an infinite diversity. And we shall find many other things in this condition, so do not trust this argument which makes all the most opposite things one.’ This, then, is the passage about colours and figures.

And the passage about pleasures is this: ‘We say that the licentious man takes pleasure, and that the temperate man too takes pleasure in the very fact of being temperate; and again that the foolish man, full of foolish opinions and hopes, takes pleasure, and again [213] that the wise man too takes pleasure in the very fact of being wise; and how could anyone who says that each of these pleasures is like the other not justly appear foolish?’ And just as Plato indicated the differences of pleasures briefly in this passage, but went through them at greater length through the whole book, so too those of the arts in two books, the Sophist and the Statesman. Are there, then, many differences of sciences and of pleasures, and of colours and figures and of the pitches in sounds, and likewise too of ages and seasons and regions and diseases, and of all other things, but in hot things alone they either do not exist at all or are impossible for human beings to know? And indeed Lycus’ argument abolishes the differences of the hot, of it alone, as he thinks, but in truth, together with all the others, if indeed the force of the argument can be extended correspondingly in the same way. For in fact I shall say the following next about moist things themselves as well, asserting that these too do not differ from one another insofar as they are moist. But the very greatest of his errors is this.

That it also abolishes all the arts, [214] which have their constitution in the differences of the species. Plato, then, having first spoken in summary about the constitution of the arts, also went through the argument by way of an example, showing how the art of grammar was constituted once the difference in sounds had been recognised. But Lycus’ argument evidently abolishes this art too, and music likewise with it, and all the others, in requiring that the ‘insofar as it is conceived’ and the ‘in some respect’ have one difference in it. Observe, at any rate, how his argument will abolish first the art concerned with letters, and after this all the others as well: ‘It seems to me impossible and impracticable that sound, for one who considers this at least insofar as it is conceived, I mean in respect of the utterance itself, should have any variation with respect to another sound, varying according to some peculiarity in quality residing in the utterance.’
uncertain_greek: ἀξιῶν τὸ ᾗ νενόηται, τὸ δέ τι μίαν ἔχειν ἐν αὐτῷ διαφοράν

response.translation: This argument is in every respect the same as the one written by Lycus at the beginning of his passage, and it is carried through by means of those very words of his, all of them, with only one, the name of ‘hot’, changed into that of ‘sound’; [215] so that if that one is valid, so too is this; but surely this one is not valid, so that neither is that one, unless perhaps those who hold Lycus’ views think that neither is the sound e different from o, nor does o differ from ō. But if we shall agree that these too are different from one another, and in addition to these a and i and u, and all the other letters, these will be twenty-four in number. And the art that knows their difference is grammar, just as the art of music too concerns the highness and lowness in sounds; and yet Lycus’ argument abolishes these no less. For sound differs in nothing from sound insofar as it is sound; but nonetheless the note of the mese is higher by a tone than that of the lichanos of the mesai, and lower by a tone than that of the paramese. And of those in turn, the note of the lichanos is higher by a tone than that of the parhypate of the mesai; while that of the paramese is lower by a semitone than that of the trite of the diezeugmenai.
